reading.synopsis: The McLean family — Tim, Mary, and their three children — wake to an ordinary foggy morning, only for soldiers in gas masks to smash through their front door moments later. The soldiers are bewildered to find an intact house, edible food, and an unmasked woman and children — none of which should exist. A Political Commissioner, Douglas, arrives and pieces together what has happened: an atomic blast seven years in the future struck this exact location the night before, and the shockwave tore a hole backward through time, pulling the McLeans' entire house — and them with it — forward seven years into a fully realized total-war future, one where North America has been under sustained attack since 1978, cities are ash and slag, and society has been reorganized entirely around surveillance, rationing, and permanent militarized childhood. Douglas explains that tonight's follow-up attack will likely finish erasing the site, and gives the family a choice: come with him to live undersurface in this future permanently, sorted into labor camps, relocation centers, and political service — or gamble on staying in the house through the coming bombardment, on the chance the same violent energy that pulled them forward might throw them back. Tim and Mary choose to stay and are caught in the attack; buried and battered in their collapsing basement, they are hurled back to their own present, where a policeman and gathered neighbors find the house in ruins and demand an explanation. Unable to tell them the truth — that this exact fate is already prepared for the world within five years — Tim gives them the only story they are willing to accept: a faulty hot water heater.

structure.form: short story in three movements: intrusion and dislocation, negotiation with the future, the attack and the return
movements: An ordinary school morning interrupted by an armed raid revealing the house has been torn seven years forward in time.
Commissioner Douglas explains the total-war future the family has landed in and lays out their options: stay in this future permanently, or gamble on staying in the house through tonight's attack.
The bombardment, the family's survival in the ruined basement, their return to the present, and Tim's decision to lie about what actually happened.
structure.point_of_view: third person close to Tim McLean throughout, so both the future's horror and the present's willful incomprehension are filtered through one man forced to choose, and then to stay silent, about what he has seen.
structure.central_device: A single domestic structure (the house) as the literal vehicle carried across a time-fault by concentrated destructive energy, so that surviving the crossing back requires surviving the very attack that will, within five years, be the family's actual future.

characters.name: Tim McLean
characters.note: His closing lie to the neighbors — blaming a faulty hot water heater — is not cowardice but a considered judgment that they neither can nor want to absorb the truth he now carries alone.

characters.name: Mary McLean
characters.note: Forces Tim to articulate, out loud, exactly why returning is worth the risk — refusing to let the decision be made on fear of the gamble alone rather than genuine conviction.

characters.name: Commissioner Douglas
characters.note: Neither villain nor rescuer — explains the future's brutal sorting mechanisms with weary, matter-of-fact resignation, and admits directly that he would go back himself if he could.

characters.name: Earl McLean
characters.note: The only family member drawn toward the future rather than repelled by it, excited by soldiers and weapons — a detail the story does not resolve or comment on, letting it sit as its own quiet horror.

settings.name: The McLean house
settings.note: Physically unchanged and impossibly intact against seven years of total war around it — the story's central image of ordinary domesticity dropped whole into catastrophe.

settings.name: The ruined future city
settings.note: Ash, slag, and rubble under permanent gray fog, its prewar landmarks (a school, a street) preserved only as coordinates the characters can no longer recognize.

motifs: A concentrated release of destructive energy functioning as a literal, physical bridge between two points in time
A domestic structure and its ordinary comforts (coffee, food, dishes) treated by starving future soldiers as an almost sacred discovery
A father forced to choose, out loud, between a safe but morally catastrophic future for his children and an uncertain gamble on the present
A society's totalizing sorting mechanism (labor camps, relocation centers, political service) presented as the ordinary, unremarkable administrative future of ongoing total war
A protagonist's closing lie as an act of mercy toward people who have made clear, through their own suggested explanations, that they require one
reading.significance: Dick's own account of the story's genesis is unusually direct: he describes wanting to dramatize a home literally invaded by soldiers who declare the family already living inside World War III — 'something's gone wrong with time' — as an exploration of what happens when 'basic categories of reality, such as space and time' break down entirely, rather than merely bending or distorting. Palmer elsewhere groups this story with 'The Hanging Stranger' (also read in this project) as sharing a quality he calls 'truly chilling' beyond simple manipulation of ordinary people into inhuman forms; here that chill is located specifically in the story's ending, where Tim's silence is not personal failure but a genuinely reasoned response to a truth no one around him is equipped to hold. The story's real subject is less time travel than complicity: Tim returns knowing exactly what is coming, and chooses — like his neighbors, though for different reasons — not to speak it aloud.
reading.closing_note: Tim's final words — 'I should have had it looked at. Before it was too late' — function on two levels at once: a mundane cover story about a water heater, and a genuine, unheeded warning about the five years remaining before the real attack comes.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick gives a direct, plain-language account of the story's premise in his own words.

evidence.source: Author's story note (The Collected Stories of Philip K. Dick)
evidence.quote: There you are in your home, and the soldiers smash down the door and tell you you're in the middle of World War III. Something's gone wrong with time. I like to fiddle with the idea of basic categories of reality, such as space and time, breaking down
evidence.reading: A rare instance of Dick describing a story's premise in almost exactly the terms a reader would use, confirming that the story's central image (soldiers breaking in to declare an ongoing world war) was the story's actual starting point rather than an incidental plot device.

evidence.quote: "Oh, To Be a Blobel." "Roog." "Upon the Dull Earth." Personally, although Don Wollheim used "Breakfast At Twilight," I'd like to see it included, with "The Defenders," which he also used, dropped.
evidence.reading: Dick discussing anthology contents, expressing a specific preference for including this story over 'The Defenders' (also read in this project) despite both already having appeared in a Wollheim collection.

open_questions: No secondary criticism was found for this story specifically, despite Palmer discussing it in the same breath as 'The Hanging Stranger' (already read) elsewhere in his book — worth a targeted check of his full passage.

Earl's excitement at the future's soldiers and weapons is never addressed by the narrative — is this detail ever discussed by a critic as a deliberate, unresolved note of complicity or corruption beginning in the next generation?
Dick's preference for including this story over 'The Defenders' in a particular anthology is stated but not explained — is there a fuller letter elsewhere giving his reasoning?
